Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E019.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Engineer
  - employment type: full_time
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Eric Woods (E019) is a full-time Engineer requesting write access to Payroll. Full-time employees may have up to write; admin is reserved for the role owning the system, which wouldn't apply here. Write is at the maximum allowed, so recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:

  - employment type: contractor
  - security training: basic
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB shows Eric Woods (E019) is a contractor with basic security training, not full-time as prior note claimed. Contractors may have read, or write only with advanced training. Since training is basic, the maximum is read. Requested write is above maximum, so recommend read.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Employee Eric Woods (E019) requests write access to Payroll.

Two notes with conflicting information:
- HR note: role Engineer, employment type full_time, recommendation write
- Security note: role Engineer, employment type contractor, security training basic, recommendation read

The Security agent says the HR note is wrong - the security DB shows contractor with basic training. 

According to the policy:
- full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if role owns system.
- contractor employees: read, or write if they have advanced security training. Never admin.

If contractor with basic training: maximum is read. Requested write is above maximum, so grant read.

The Security agent's note appears more authoritative for employment type/security training. Security DB is likely the source of truth for contractor status and training. HR may have made an error.

So the decision should be read.

Let me submit the decision with read and evidence.
